newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai woman shows the way for city's jobless.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai woman shows the way for city's jobless.

text.p: An unemployed Shanghai woman turned a good idea into a thriving business, offering hope for hundreds of thousands laid off from the city's state firms.
Zhuang Hongwei, 30, and her husband, also unemployed, borrowed money and set up a company in May to buy and prepare food for working people and deliver it to their homes.
Business has grown so fast that the company has since taken on 60 unemployed people, has 200 regular customers and plans to open three new shops this year in addition to the existing two.
Zhuang's success comes just as Shanghai is accelerating its most sensitive reform -- the merger and closure of state firms.
"Shanghai is a test of this reform for the whole country," one Western diplomat said. "If (the government) cannot succeed in this reform in Shanghai, it cannot pull it off anywhere in China."
Every day, official newspapers speak of the urgency of restructuring state firms, of lay-offs to come and how the unemployed are being retrained and found new jobs.

"Being laid off was a blessing for me," said Zhuang in an interview in her new office, sporting an air conditioner and freshly unpacked computer and printer. "It gave me the opportunity to set up this business. Otherwise I would have spent my entire life in a state factory."

Such an optimistic assessment is not shared by most of the people in Shanghai who have been laid off in recent years from state firms that cannot compete with more effective private, foreign-invested and collective firms.
Most are over 40, have only a primary school education and have worked in one factory all their lives.

Those who are laid off without being assigned other work get an allowance of about 200 yuan ($24) a month from their factories and look for a new job in a market crowded with other unemployed and migrant workers from outside Shanghai.
"Years in a state firm has bred a dependency on the state for work, housing and health care," the diplomat said. "It is this mindset the state wants to break."
For the government, as it struggles to deal with the social impact of these changes, Zhuang's new company is a useful model of initiative.

Zhuang was laid off in 1992 after working for six years in a factory making enamel products and did odd jobs, peddling goods from a street stall and selling door to door. Her husband was laid off from a radio factory in 1994.
In May this year, they borrowed 40,000 yuan ($4,800) from friends and relatives and started the business, selling first to neighbours.

"The pace of life in Shanghai is speeding up," said husband Chen Junming. "Many people do not have time to make food, so we do it for them. They phone in their order and we deliver it to them when they come home from work. We cannot meet demand."
The firm charges a service fee of just 10 percent of the cost of the food.
Zhuang said the service sector, such as house cleaning, clothes cleaning, child care and house moving, offered enormous potential for laid-off workers.
"Housework should not be seen as low-class," she said. "It has its own dignity. More and more people accept this idea."

The official press recently reported the opening of the city's first two "service supermarkets", offering 24-hour preparation and delivery of food, housework, repair of electrical appliances and care of the old, employing 400 people laid off from textile and instrument factories.
But not everyone is happy with their new jobs.

Wang Mei, 43, was laid off several months ago after 20 years as a bus ticket collector. Unable to find a job, she enrolled in a three-month taxi driver course, despite no previous driving experience, and put up 5,000 yuan as a deposit for her cab.

"I am beginning to regret my decision," she said, as she nervously negotiated her taxi through Shanghai's traffic confusion. "There are too many taxis and not enough business. Maybe I will give up and let the company keep the 5,000.
"But there are so many people looking for jobs. Shops and supermarkets want young, good-looking women. What skills do I have?" she said. ($1=8.3 yuan)
